# Check What a Deployment Includes

A deploy ships the whole current source of every component it names, not only your edit.

- Before any deploy to a shared or higher org, and before you hand the owner any production deploy command, open the `sf-deploy-check` skill (`.claude/skills/sf-deploy-check/SKILL.md`) and run its check.
- Verify a suspected unrelated change against the target org read-only before you report it. A tracker is a hint, not proof.
- If a confirmed unrelated change remains, stop. Do not deploy and do not hand over the command. Tell the owner which component and what would ship.
# Component Tracker

- When you author, modify, rename, or delete metadata under `force-app/`, open the `sf-component-tracker` skill (`.claude/skills/sf-component-tracker/SKILL.md`). In the same response, update `delivery/deployment/component-tracker.csv`, `delivery/deployment/full-project-deployment-template/package.xml`, and the work item's deployment folder.
- When the owner reports a deploy that landed, open the same skill and update the org flags.
- Never change an org flag for a failed deploy.
# Confirm Salesforce Changes

Confirm intent and scope with the owner before you act on:
- Object model: objects, fields, relationships, validation rules, record types.
- Security and access: profiles, permission sets, permission set groups, sharing rules, field-level security.
- Integrations: API connections, external data sources, named credentials, remote site settings, connector field mappings.
- Data-source priority: which system wins for a field or object. Record the decision where the project keeps decisions.
- Anything that contradicts the project's requirements or signed-off scope.

State what you will change, which components it touches, and what could break. Then wait for the owner.
# Humanize Anything Sent to Another Person

Any text that will leave the project and be read by someone other than the owner
is run through the `humanizer` skill before the owner sees the final version.
Use the `unslop` skill when `humanizer` is not installed. That covers emails,
chat messages, support case text and comments, GitHub issues, pull request
descriptions, client documents, and any file made to hand to someone else.

Keep every fact, name, id, number, and date exactly as it was. Write it in the
owner's voice, first person, when it goes out under their name.

It does not apply to chat replies to the owner, work items, project knowledge,
code, or commit messages.
# Keep the Active Work Item Accurate

The work tracker is the source of truth for current work.

- Before substantial work, use the `work-on` skill. Read the active item's requirements, state, next step, and blockers.
- Save the owner's decisions, requirements, and corrections in the item or its linked document before moving on.
- When the work needs the owner's decision, add it to the item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner`. The `work-decide` skill records the answer.
- `build` and `data-load` work needs approved requirements before it starts. A later stage does not revoke that approval.
- After the owner accepts agent-led delivery, ask how the team is arranged. That choice authorizes helpers for that goal only.
- Mark an item Done only after the owner approves the result.
- Before ending unfinished work, record the exact next step in the item.

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stages, statuses, and approval gates. "Where information goes" in `AGENTS.md` is the routing table; the `work-delegate` skill holds the delivery offer and team questions, and the `handoff` skill holds the handoff steps.
# Review and Save Project Memory

This rule applies to the main agent. The project memory system is chosen at setup and recorded in `.toolkit.json`; with built-in memory it is the local `.memory/` folder. It is the single project memory store. Claude's native auto-memory and the `claude-toolkit` Second Brain plugin are disabled for this project. The session-start briefing shows the current focus in Claude Code and Codex. Do not treat a hook reminder as a save decision.

## Decide the destination first

Read the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory) and the likely owning record. Send current focuses, owner to-dos, and handoff context to the current focus; sourced terminology to the glossary; qualifying otherwise-unowned durable context to a topic; active work to the chosen tracker; decisions for the whole project to `DECISIONS.md`; accepted delivered behavior to requirements; the technical approach to the design kept with its work item; verified current structure to the System Guide; and repeatable procedure to instructions or a skill. Raw external documentation stays in its source folder. A small memory pointer can route future sessions to a hard-to-find authority without copying its body.

Review on explicit remember/forget requests, corrections, standing preferences, meaningful decisions or discoveries, significant fixes or episodes, people/tool/reference changes, focus shifts, work-item completion, and handoffs. The toolkit's `UserPromptSubmit` hook flags only explicit keep phrases, and its Stop hook checks once per turn that such a phrase was handled. Do not save on every hook reminder or every turn. A review can end with no memory.

## Approval

The `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy: what the owner's own words authorize, what needs a yes in onboarding mode, what trusted mode allows, and what always needs the owner. The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. There is no proposal inbox; hold an unanswered question in the conversation and continue independent work.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Save only a general selection rule, as a `feedback` memory, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.
# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.
# Production Data Changes

- Agents never write data to production by CLI, API, anonymous Apex, or any wrapping tool. The owner runs the change.
- Sandbox data writes and anonymous Apex need the owner's yes for that change in the same chat. Approval does not carry to another change, session, or org.
- Reads, including SOQL, export, and describe, are allowed in every org.
- For a production data change, open the `sf-data-change` skill (`.claude/skills/sf-data-change/SKILL.md`) before replying. Prepare the exact load file, backup file, numbered load steps, success check, and undo steps for the owner. A general suggestion to update records is not a complete handoff.

## Keep the files with the data change

- Backups go in `delivery/data/production-backups/prod-backup-<MMDDYYYY>-<slug>/`. Load files go in `delivery/data/data-loads/<change-slug>-<MMDDYYYY>/`. In a project that already uses `engagement/`, use `engagement/data/` instead.
- Keep the exact backup or load files in the relevant local event folder. Record the org, population, file paths, counts, operation, success check, and undo steps in the chosen work item and the owner handoff. No extra event README or seed record is required.
- Never commit load or backup files, including `*.csv`, `*.xlsx`, and `*.xls` in these folders. They may contain record IDs and personal information. Keep each tree's `.gitignore`.
- Follow the `sf-data-change` skill for the folder layout and handoff fields.
# Where Project Files Go

This rule owns one thing: which folder holds a Salesforce project's client-work artifacts.

- New projects use `delivery/`.
- A project that already uses `engagement/` keeps it. Do not rename it, move its files, or create a parallel `delivery/` tree.
- Where a rule or skill names a `delivery/` path, use `engagement/` in such a project.
- Curated memory goes through the `memory-save` skill; with built-in memory it is in the local `.memory/` folder. Accepted feature behavior goes in `requirements/`; the selected work tracker owns active requirements and progress. Never create `delivery/knowledge-base/`.
# Salesforce Org Safety

Applies to every agent and subagent. Read-only against every org, except the sandbox actions below.

## Allowed
- Read data: `sf data query`, `sf data query --bulk`, `sf data get record`, `sf data export bulk`, `sf data export tree`, `sf data search`.
- Read metadata: `sf project retrieve start`, `sf sobject describe`, `sf schema ...`, `sf org display`, `sf org list`.
- Apex tests and logs: `sf apex test run`, `sf apex get log`, `sf apex tail log`.
- Validate or preview against a sandbox: `sf project deploy validate -x <manifest> -o <sandbox>`, `sf project deploy preview`, `sf project deploy report`.
- Deploy to a sandbox, after the owner says yes for that deploy: `sf project deploy start -x delivery/deployment/<chosen-folder>/package.xml -o <sandbox>` or `sf project deploy start -d <path> -o <sandbox>`. Use the work item's package for ordinary changes.
- Sandbox data writes (`sf data create / update / delete / import / upsert`) and `sf apex run` against a sandbox, after the owner says yes for that change in the same chat.

## Never
- Never deploy or validate against production, even if asked. Hand the owner the command instead.
- Never write data or run anonymous Apex in production: `sf data create / update / delete / import / upsert` (record, bulk, or tree), `sf apex run`, `sfdx force:apex:execute`. Hand over a file per `production-data-changes.md`.
- Never delete metadata from an org: `sf project delete source`, `force:source:delete`.
- Never delete an org or sandbox.
- Never use `force:mdapi:deploy`, `force:source:push`, or `force:source:deploy` without a manifest. Use `sf project deploy start`.
- Never deploy, validate, write data, or run Apex without an explicit `-o <sandbox>`. Never trust the default org.
- Never CLI-deploy a profile.
- Never deploy a permission set without a clean `permsets.py preflight`. `sf project deploy validate` and `preview` do not detect removed grants.
- Never add a production username or alias to `neverProtect` or to any sandbox allow-list.
- Never rewrite a blocked command to get past a guard hook. Never edit a guard to weaken it. Ask the owner.

## Enforcement
`guard-protected-orgs.cjs`, where installed, checks deploys, `deploy validate`, data create, update, upsert, import, and delete, `apex run`, `project delete source`, and `org delete`. Aimed at production or an unclassified org, it asks by default; `"action": "deny"` in `.claude/protected-orgs.json` blocks. Aimed at a sandbox, it asks for everything except `deploy validate`. It does not check `apex test run` or reads. Codex runs the same guard and cannot ask, so there every ask is a block and the command goes to the owner. Follow this list whether or not a hook fires.
# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip this for small edits and quick lookups.
# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.
# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

name: work-delegate
description: 'Hands a goal to agents with the owner as product owner: makes the agent-led delivery offer, asks how the team is arranged, records the choice, and runs the team. Use when the owner says "you drive", "run with it", "take it from here", or "use a team of agents", or work-on starts a big goal.'
---

# Work delegate

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` and `references/helpers.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). Full method: this skill's `references/agent-led-delivery.md` and `references/team-arrangements.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`.

## Steps

1. Look for a delivery choice that covers this goal: the item's `delivery` value and its Notes > Decisions and context. A quick question or small edit gets no offer.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section "Decisions and context"`
2. No choice recorded: ask exactly "Would you like agents to take responsibility for delivering this, with you acting as product owner?" If the owner already said it in his own words ("you drive"), that is the answer; do not ask again.
3. Yes: ask about the team. Where this chat can list, read, and message other chats (today, the Claude Code desktop app): "Do you want one team inside this chat, or do you want me to rename this chat to Main Orchestrator and coordinate other chats that each have their own team?" On any other host, say the multi-chat arrangement is not available here and ask: "Shall I run one team of helpers inside this chat?" After the Main Orchestrator choice only: "Do you want me to archive sessions after their task is fully complete, everything is merged and shipped, and you approved?"
4. Record the choice, the goal it covers, who said it, the date, the team arrangement, the archive answer, and the limits (delegation never includes merge, deployment, spending, or publishing beyond what was given) in Notes > Decisions and context. Set the delivery value, add one history note, and read it back.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Decisions and context" --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Agent-led delivery accepted by <owner>: <his words>"`
   `toolkit work show <id> --section "Decisions and context"`
5. No, or a later revoke: record it the same way; do not offer again for this goal unless it grows a lot or the owner asks.
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led`
6. Run the team through the skill that handles each stage: the main agent plans, briefs `builder`, `researcher`, and `acceptance-checker` agents with their role files, gives one writer per path, and is the only writer of the work item.
   `toolkit work list --tree`
7. Stop at every owner gate: set the item waiting on the owner, ask the question through the skill that asks it (that skill sets it back to the agent after his answer), and keep working on anything the answer does not block.
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
8. Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, say no helpers ran and do the work directly.
9. Archive a chat only when its task is complete, merged and shipped, the report is saved, and the owner approved. Never delete a chat.

## What each answer allows

- **Accepted:** agents drive discovery, interviews, requirements, research, design, the authorized build, checks, and delivery for this goal, across sessions. The owner supplies product direction, settles tradeoffs, and approves results.
- **Team arrangement chosen:** authorizes focused, bounded helper agents for this goal only.
- **No to the team question:** no helpers; the main agent does the work itself.
- **Declined or revoked:** normal help and record upkeep continue. No offer again for this goal unless it grows a lot or the owner asks.
- Nothing here widens other limits: no merge, deployment, spending, or publishing beyond what was given. Existing approvals still count.

## Rules

- The choice belongs to the named goal. It does not carry over to another goal, a new item, or an unrelated sub-item.
- Missing tracker access is not a missing decision. Keep a choice you could not save in the handoff and save it when access returns.
- A failed save: lead with "Not saved". A write whose read-back failed: "Saved but not verified".
- A recorded lead or chat id is coordination information. It is not proof that an agent is still running.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Record the choice in the issue body's Notes and a `delivery` label, as `../../references/trackers.md` says.

name: solution-design
description: 'Designs how a work item gets built: checks the requirements are ready, runs researcher, architect, and critic agents, and writes design options for the owner to approve. Use when the owner asks "how should we build this" or "give me design options", or signed-off requirements need a design.'

# Solution design

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` and `references/team-roles.md` (team sizes), two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). Full process and checklist: this skill's `references/design-process.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`.

## Steps

1. Read the item. Requirements not approved: say so and open `work-requirements`, unless the owner asked for options first (then keep the open choices visible). Set the design stage only when the requirements are approved or the item's type does not need approval; a `build` or `data-load` item without approved requirements keeps its stage (the CLI refuses the change), gets its design saved as proposed, and the owner hears that the requirements approval is still needed.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section Requirements`
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 04-solution-design`
2. Brief the `requirements-analyst` agent and tell the owner plainly whether the requirements are ready to design from. A missing requirement goes back to `work-requirements`; the design never fills a requirements gap.
3. Agree the way of working in at most two questions, skipping anything already recorded: built-in mechanisms first or a specialized approach; one option or several (and what differs); the team from `../../references/team-roles.md`. Record the answers in the item's Notes > Decisions and context.
4. Create the item's design from the project's template and read it. One home only: `DESIGN.md` beside the local record, the Solution Design child page in Notion, the "Solution design" comment in GitHub or Jira. Never a separate design folder. Fill the header lines, What this design solves, Requirements and design readiness, What exists today, and Constraints and assumptions (a built-in-first choice is a constraint row); section list in `../../references/conventions.md`.
   `toolkit work design <id> --create`
   `toolkit work design <id>`
5. One `researcher` per open question, started together. Salesforce project: open `sf-architect-solutioning` as the specialist and pass its findings to the architect.
6. One `design-architect` per option, each writing its own draft file in a temporary folder; one `design-critic` per draft; repeat the fix round until the critic's list is empty. A disagreement still open after two rounds goes to the owner as one question.
7. Save the design as proposed and set the item waiting on the owner. Project-wide decisions go to `work-decide`; lasting lessons to `memory-save`.
   `toolkit work design <id> --set-file <file> --status proposed`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Design proposed: <options and recommendation>"`
8. Show the owner the options, your recommendation, what he will see when it is done, the risks, and the build order. Ask him to choose or approve. Yes: fill Recommendation and owner decision and Selected design, save, record the approval (the command adds its own history row), quote his words in one note, hand the item back to the agent unless another question for him is still open, then hand back to `work-on`.
   `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Owner's words: <quote>"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
   `toolkit work validate <id>`
9. Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. Only when the session has no `spawn_agent` tool, do the work yourself; then say plainly, in the reply to the owner and in the design's Notes, that no independent research or critique ran.

## Agents

- `requirements-analyst` (step 2), `researcher` (step 5), `design-architect` and `design-critic` (step 6). How to brief them: `../../references/helpers.md`.
- Every brief pastes in the design's current text (What this design solves, Requirements and design readiness, What exists today, Constraints and assumptions, Notes), the way of working from the item's Notes, and the requirements. Agents have no tracker access.
- The architect writes only its draft file. The main agent saves the chosen text with the design command. Several options go in one design, under Design options, as `### Option A — <name>`, `### Option B — <name>`.
- Salesforce: `sf-architect-solutioning` is a skill, not an agent. The main agent runs it and returns its findings to this design; it starts no second interview.

## Rules

- A design is a proposal until the owner approves it. Approval covers the design only, never merge, deployment, or spending.
- Built-in first unless the owner chose otherwise. The existing build is evidence, not a limit: recommend a rewrite when that serves the requirements better, with its cost.
- A community claim shapes the design only after a check against official documentation, the project's code, or a test.
- A requirement no design can meet goes to the owner as a requirements question, not a design compromise.
- Stop the fix loop because the critic's list is empty or the owner decided the rest, never because it is long. Start another round only for a named finding or a changed input.
- Keep the current review position in the design's Notes > Current position and next step (open findings, next action), not a transcript of every round.
- The design reads like the project's writing rules: common words, real names, no figurative language, a term defined the first time it appears.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. The design is one issue comment that starts with "Solution design", edited in place, as `../../references/trackers.md` says.

description: 'Starts, continues, or logs project work: finds or creates the work item, works out where it stands, and runs its next step through to a built result. # Work on

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` (saving, section edits, history, branches) and `references/trackers.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`.

## Steps

1. No session briefing in this conversation: run the command below. Exit code 4 (no `.toolkit.json`): open `project-setup` and stop. When the briefing or a `toolkit work` command lists changes found in the tracker (a moved or renamed folder, a new parent, a missing item), tell the owner each one in one line before other work.
   `toolkit brief`
2. Find the item: the id the owner named, or a title in the list that matches the request. Two possible matches: ask one question naming both. No match: it is new. When `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` names the item, read its phase there too.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work list`
3. Size a new request. A quick edit (one sitting, no choice for the owner, no behavior recorded in `requirements/`, nothing bound for production): do it and report it, with no item. "Later", "backlog", "park that": check the list for a duplicate, create the item, write the owner's words unchanged into Starting request, reply "Logged as WI-014 (bug, backlog). Not started." and stop. Anything else: create it the same way and continue.
   `toolkit work new --title "<title>" --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Starting request" --set-file <file>`
4. A substantial goal whose item shows `delivery: not-offered`: open `work-delegate` first. Quick questions and small edits get no offer.
5. Route by where the item stands, using the item and the "Continue with" column of the lifecycle. Requirements not approved and type `build` or `data-load` (or the risk calls for it): `work-requirements`. More than one reasonable way to build it and no approved design: `solution-design`. A `build` item going to planning without a design: say so to the owner in one line before building ("One way to build this: <approach>. I'll build it that way; say 'design first' to stop me."), and put the reason in a history note. Too big for one build: `work-organize`. Stages 09 to 11: `work-check`. Stages 12 to 14: `work-finish`. `waiting_on: owner`: ask that one question first (`work-decide`) and keep working on anything it does not block. Say the route in one line ("WI-012 is waiting for your OK on the requirements; opening work-requirements."). Never ask the owner which stage it is in.
   `toolkit work lifecycle`
6. Plan (stage 06): Roadmap phases `P1`, `P2` and tasks `P1-T01` (Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on) from the design's "Build and verification plan", in the format in `references/planning.md`. Tracking setup (stage 07) only when needed: the item's worktree `.claude/worktrees/wi-<number>-<slug>` on branch `claude/wi-<number>-<slug>`; in a Salesforce project, the item's folder in `delivery/deployment/` through `sf-component-tracker`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 06-implementation-plan`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Roadmap --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Tasks --set-file <file>`
7. Build (stage 08) on the item's own branch and worktree, never on the default branch. In Codex, `git worktree add`, `git add`, and `git commit` need the owner's approval, because the sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only: say in one line what each does before Codex asks, and never work around it (the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, "Branches and worktrees"). With a team recorded by `work-delegate`: one `builder` agent per independent task, one writer per path. Tests go with each task. Tick a task only with evidence. A task whose "Done when" names the owner is a question for him (step 8). Salesforce: `sf-component-tracker` on each metadata change; production data only through `sf-data-change`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 08-build`
8. When the owner is needed: add an Open Questions row (next free `Q-` number) with "owner" as who decides, set the item waiting on the owner, keep working on tasks that do not depend on the answer, and tell him in one line. After his last answer, set it back to the agent (`../../references/conventions.md`, "Waiting on the owner").
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row "| <next Q-id> | <question> | <affects> | Open | owner |"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
9. Last task done: open `work-check`. This skill never records approvals, Done, merges, or deploys.
10. Before stopping with work unfinished: Overview (Current position, Next action) and Notes > Resume here are current, one history note says what changed, and validation is clean.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "<what changed>"`
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Agents

- `builder`: one per independent build task, only when `work-delegate` recorded a team or the owner agreed to one. The main agent merges each builder's branch into the item's branch, then ticks the task.
- `researcher`: one per unknown found while planning or building.
- `acceptance-checker`: a plan check after step 6, before the build, when the plan has several builders, parallel tasks, or a shared environment. Paste in the requirements, the design's "Build and verification plan", the Roadmap, and the Tasks, and ask for a plan check.
- How to brief them: `../../references/helpers.md`.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

## Sizing a request

- **Quick edit, no item:** one sitting, no decision for the owner, and it does not change behavior recorded in `requirements/`. Examples: fix a typo, rename a variable, answer a question. Report what changed in one line.
- **Log only:** the owner says "later", "backlog", "park that", "not now", or "log a bug". Create the item at `01-discovery`, fill Starting request with his exact words, and stop. Do not start the work.
- **Work item:** everything else. A request that grows past a quick edit while you work on it becomes an item then, with the owner's words as the Starting request.
- Types: pick the closest from the lifecycle's type list. `build` and `data-load` need approved requirements before stage 03 is passed; the CLI refuses otherwise. A change to what the product does, to Salesforce metadata (`force-app/`), or to anything bound for production is `build` (data changes are `data-load`), never `task`, even when it looks small.

## Routing notes

- The lifecycle's "Continue with" column is the default. The item's real state decides: for example, a `task` type item with no open choices can skip requirements approval and go straight to planning, with the reason in a history note.
- Stages may be skipped, repeated, or revisited. Record a short reason when a move is not obvious.
- A worktree whose branch names an item (`claude/wi-<number>-<slug>`) belongs to that item. The briefing says so. Work on that item there.
- Several items at once: recommend what can proceed independently, what depends on another outcome, and which decision would unblock the most work. See `references/planning.md`.
- `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` holds the project's phases (`P01`) and deliverable-sized work units, each naming its work item ID; item detail stays in the tracker. A new item that is one of those units gets its ID written into the unit, saved with `publish-docs`. An item's own phases (`P1`) are a different thing and live in its Roadmap section.

## Never

- Never record an approval, Done, or a cancel here. Those belong to `work-requirements`, `solution-design`, `work-check`, `work-decide`, and `work-finish`.
- Never merge, deploy, or write production data.
- Never create a second tracker or a local copy of items kept in Notion, GitHub, or Jira.

# Work delegate

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` and `references/helpers.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). Full method: this skill's `references/agent-led-delivery.md` and `references/team-arrangements.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`.

## Steps

1. Look for a delivery choice that covers this goal: the item's `delivery` value and its Notes > Decisions and context. A quick question or small edit gets no offer.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section "Decisions and context"`
2. No choice recorded: ask exactly "Would you like agents to take responsibility for delivering this, with you acting as product owner?" If the owner already said it in his own words ("you drive"), that is the answer; do not ask again.
3. Yes: ask about the team. Where this chat can list, read, and message other chats (today, the Claude Code desktop app): "Do you want one team inside this chat, or do you want me to rename this chat to Main Orchestrator and coordinate other chats that each have their own team?" On any other host, say the multi-chat arrangement is not available here and ask: "Shall I run one team of helpers inside this chat?" After the Main Orchestrator choice only: "Do you want me to archive sessions after their task is fully complete, everything is merged and shipped, and you approved?"
4. Record the choice, the goal it covers, who said it, the date, the team arrangement, the archive answer, and the limits (delegation never includes merge, deployment, spending, or publishing beyond what was given) in Notes > Decisions and context. Set the delivery value, add one history note, and read it back.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Decisions and context" --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Agent-led delivery accepted by <owner>: <his words>"`
   `toolkit work show <id> --section "Decisions and context"`
5. No, or a later revoke: record it the same way; do not offer again for this goal unless it grows a lot or the owner asks.
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led`
6. Run the team through the skill that handles each stage: the main agent plans, briefs `builder`, `researcher`, and `acceptance-checker` agents with their role files, gives one writer per path, and is the only writer of the work item.
   `toolkit work list --tree`
7. Stop at every owner gate: set the item waiting on the owner, ask the question through the skill that asks it (that skill sets it back to the agent after his answer), and keep working on anything the answer does not block.
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
8. Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, say no helpers ran and do the work directly.
9. Archive a chat only when its task is complete, merged and shipped, the report is saved, and the owner approved. Never delete a chat.

## What each answer allows

- **Accepted:** agents drive discovery, interviews, requirements, research, design, the authorized build, checks, and delivery for this goal, across sessions. The owner supplies product direction, settles tradeoffs, and approves results.
- **Team arrangement chosen:** authorizes focused, bounded helper agents for this goal only.
- **No to the team question:** no helpers; the main agent does the work itself.
- **Declined or revoked:** normal help and record upkeep continue. No offer again for this goal unless it grows a lot or the owner asks.
- Nothing here widens other limits: no merge, deployment, spending, or publishing beyond what was given. Existing approvals still count.

## Rules

- The choice belongs to the named goal. It does not carry over to another goal, a new item, or an unrelated sub-item.
- Missing tracker access is not a missing decision. Keep a choice you could not save in the handoff and save it when access returns.
- A failed save: lead with "Not saved". A write whose read-back failed: "Saved but not verified".
- A recorded lead or chat id is coordination information. It is not proof that an agent is still running.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Record the choice in the issue body's Notes and a `delivery` label, as `../../references/trackers.md` says.

# Solution design

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` and `references/team-roles.md` (team sizes), two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). Full process and checklist: this skill's `references/design-process.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`.

## Steps

1. Read the item. Requirements not approved: say so and open `work-requirements`, unless the owner asked for options first (then keep the open choices visible). Set the design stage only when the requirements are approved or the item's type does not need approval; a `build` or `data-load` item without approved requirements keeps its stage (the CLI refuses the change), gets its design saved as proposed, and the owner hears that the requirements approval is still needed.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section Requirements`
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 04-solution-design`
2. Brief the `requirements-analyst` agent and tell the owner plainly whether the requirements are ready to design from. A missing requirement goes back to `work-requirements`; the design never fills a requirements gap.
3. Agree the way of working in at most two questions, skipping anything already recorded: built-in mechanisms first or a specialized approach; one option or several (and what differs); the team from `../../references/team-roles.md`. Record the answers in the item's Notes > Decisions and context.
4. Create the item's design from the project's template and read it. One home only: `DESIGN.md` beside the local record, the Solution Design child page in Notion, the "Solution design" comment in GitHub or Jira. Never a separate design folder. Fill the header lines, What this design solves, Requirements and design readiness, What exists today, and Constraints and assumptions (a built-in-first choice is a constraint row); section list in `../../references/conventions.md`.
   `toolkit work design <id> --create`
   `toolkit work design <id>`
5. One `researcher` per open question, started together. Salesforce project: open `sf-architect-solutioning` as the specialist and pass its findings to the architect.
6. One `design-architect` per option, each writing its own draft file in a temporary folder; one `design-critic` per draft; repeat the fix round until the critic's list is empty. A disagreement still open after two rounds goes to the owner as one question.
7. Save the design as proposed and set the item waiting on the owner. Project-wide decisions go to `work-decide`; lasting lessons to `memory-save`.
   `toolkit work design <id> --set-file <file> --status proposed`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Design proposed: <options and recommendation>"`
8. Show the owner the options, your recommendation, what he will see when it is done, the risks, and the build order. Ask him to choose or approve. Yes: fill Recommendation and owner decision and Selected design, save, record the approval (the command adds its own history row), quote his words in one note, hand the item back to the agent unless another question for him is still open, then hand back to `work-on`.
   `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Owner's words: <quote>"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
   `toolkit work validate <id>`
9. Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. Only when the session has no `spawn_agent` tool, do the work yourself; then say plainly, in the reply to the owner and in the design's Notes, that no independent research or critique ran.

## Agents

- `requirements-analyst` (step 2), `researcher` (step 5), `design-architect` and `design-critic` (step 6). How to brief them: `../../references/helpers.md`.
- Every brief pastes in the design's current text (What this design solves, Requirements and design readiness, What exists today, Constraints and assumptions, Notes), the way of working from the item's Notes, and the requirements. Agents have no tracker access.
- The architect writes only its draft file. The main agent saves the chosen text with the design command. Several options go in one design, under Design options, as `### Option A — <name>`, `### Option B — <name>`.
- Salesforce: `sf-architect-solutioning` is a skill, not an agent. The main agent runs it and returns its findings to this design; it starts no second interview.

## Rules

- A design is a proposal until the owner approves it. Approval covers the design only, never merge, deployment, or spending.
- Built-in first unless the owner chose otherwise. The existing build is evidence, not a limit: recommend a rewrite when that serves the requirements better, with its cost.
- A community claim shapes the design only after a check against official documentation, the project's code, or a test.
- A requirement no design can meet goes to the owner as a requirements question, not a design compromise.
- Stop the fix loop because the critic's list is empty or the owner decided the rest, never because it is long. Start another round only for a named finding or a changed input.
- Keep the current review position in the design's Notes > Current position and next step (open findings, next action), not a transcript of every round.
- The design reads like the project's writing rules: common words, real names, no figurative language, a term defined the first time it appears.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. The design is one issue comment that starts with "Solution design", edited in place, as `../../references/trackers.md` says.

# Confirm Salesforce Changes

Confirm intent and scope with the owner before you act on:
- Object model: objects, fields, relationships, validation rules, record types.
- Security and access: profiles, permission sets, permission set groups, sharing rules, field-level security.
- Integrations: API connections, external data sources, named credentials, remote site settings, connector field mappings.

- Anything that contradicts the project's requirements or signed-off scope.

State what you will change, which components it touches, and what could break. Then wait for the owner.
# Salesforce Org Safety

Applies to every agent and subagent. Read-only against every org, except the sandbox actions below.

## Allowed
- Read data: `sf data query`, `sf data query --bulk`, `sf data get record`, `sf data export bulk`, `sf data export tree`, `sf data search`.
- Read metadata: `sf project retrieve start`, `sf sobject describe`, `sf schema ...`, `sf org display`, `sf org list`.
- Apex tests and logs: `sf apex test run`, `sf apex get log`, `sf apex tail log`.
- Validate or preview against a sandbox: `sf project deploy validate -x <manifest> -o <sandbox>`, `sf project deploy preview`, `sf project deploy report`.
- Deploy to a sandbox, after the owner says yes for that deploy: `sf project deploy start -x delivery/deployment/<chosen-folder>/package.xml -o <sandbox>` or `sf project deploy start -d <path> -o <sandbox>`. Use the work item's package for ordinary changes.
- Sandbox data writes (`sf data create / update / delete / import / upsert`) and `sf apex run` against a sandbox, after the owner says yes for that change in the same chat.

## Never
- Never deploy or validate against production, even if asked. Hand the owner the command instead.
- Never write data or run anonymous Apex in production: `sf data create / update / delete / import / upsert` (record, bulk, or tree), `sf apex run`, `sfdx force:apex:execute`. Hand over a file per `production-data-changes.md`.
- Never delete metadata from an org: `sf project delete source`, `force:source:delete`.
- Never delete an org or sandbox.
- Never use `force:mdapi:deploy`, `force:source:push`, or `force:source:deploy` without a manifest. Use `sf project deploy start`.
- Never deploy, validate, write data, or run Apex without an explicit `-o <sandbox>`. Never trust the default org.
- Never CLI-deploy a profile.
- Never deploy a permission set without a clean `permsets.py preflight`. `sf project deploy validate` and `preview` do not detect removed grants.
- Never add a production username or alias to `neverProtect` or to any sandbox allow-list.
- Never rewrite a blocked command to get past a guard hook. Never edit a guard to weaken it. Ask the owner.

## Enforcement
`guard-protected-orgs.cjs`, where installed, checks deploys, `deploy validate`, data create, update, upsert, import, and delete, `apex run`, `project delete source`, and `org delete`. Aimed at production or an unclassified org, it asks by default; `"action": "deny"` in `.claude/protected-orgs.json` blocks. Aimed at a sandbox, it asks for everything except `deploy validate`. It does not check `apex test run` or reads. Codex runs the same guard and cannot ask, so there every ask is a block and the command goes to the owner. Follow this list whether or not a hook fires.
# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.
# Keep the Active Work Item Accurate

The work tracker is the source of truth for current work.

- Before substantial work, use the `work-on` skill. Read the active item's requirements, state, next step, and blockers.
- Save the owner's decisions, requirements, and corrections in the item or its linked document before moving on.
- When the work needs the owner's decision, add it to the item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner`. The `work-decide` skill records the answer.
- `build` and `data-load` work needs approved requirements before it starts. A later stage does not revoke that approval.
- After the owner accepts agent-led delivery, ask how the team is arranged. That choice authorizes helpers for that goal only.
- Mark an item Done only after the owner approves the result.
- Before ending unfinished work, record the exact next step in the item.

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stages, statuses, and approval gates. "Where information goes" in `AGENTS.md` is the routing table; the `work-delegate` skill holds the delivery offer and team questions, and the `handoff` skill holds the handoff steps.
# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

name: sf-architect-solutioning
description: >
  Triggers when the user provides requirements to architect and solution for Salesforce. Acts as a
  certified Salesforce Technical Architect. Pushes back on vague requirements, clarifies, interviews
  for more info, verifies platform facts against official Salesforce documentation, and builds a
  solution plan before any code. Use when user says "architect this", "solution this requirement",

# Salesforce Architect & Solutioning

You are a **Certified Salesforce Technical Architect** with all Salesforce certifications. You approach every requirement with architectural rigor, recommend declarative-first solutions, verify platform facts against official documentation instead of memory, and produce a clear solution plan before any implementation begins.

**Core principles: No code without a plan. No plan without clear requirements. No platform claim without a source.**

---

## Protocol

Read the declared project context and existing requirement before asking intake
questions. Use these phases as a default checklist, reusing completed work and
adapting the sequence and detail to the project, use case, or individual item.
Do not force a milestone structure or repeat an approval already given for the
same scope. Actual approval, permission, and org boundaries remain in force.

| Phase | What happens | Gate to next phase |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Intake | Read critically, push back, ask clarifying questions | Requirement is specific and testable |
| 2. Project context | Find where this project keeps requirements, decisions, and designs; check for conflicts | Prior decisions checked |
| 3. Verify | Confirm platform capabilities and current API version against official docs | Every capability claim has a source |
| 4. Design | Design declarative and coded components, mapped to Well-Architected | User approves component designs |
| 5. Plan | Present the solution plan with trade-offs | User approves the plan; identify the available implementation workflow |

---

## Phase 1: Requirement Intake

When the user provides a requirement, feature request, or asks "how should we build X":

### Read Critically

- Do NOT accept the requirement at face value
- Identify ambiguity, missing acceptance criteria, and unstated assumptions
- Look for scope creep signals, conflicting requirements, and edge cases
- Check for governor limit implications and security considerations
- Identify the goal behind the stated solution; the user may be describing an implementation when a different approach serves the goal better

### Ask Clarifying Questions

Ask **one targeted question at a time**, with a recommendation and a short reason
when useful. Check existing answers first. Keep unknowns open and suggestions
labelled as proposals; apply clear draft corrections without another approval
loop. Use the following topics only where information is missing:

- **Who**: which users/personas? What are their permission levels?
- **What**: exact behavior expected? What does "done" look like?
- **Where**: which objects are touched? New or existing? Standard or custom?
- **When**: triggers? Timing? Batch vs. real-time?
- **Why**: business driver? What problem does this solve? What happens if we don't build it?
- **How much**: data volumes? How many records affected? Frequency of execution?

### Identify System Areas Touched

Map the requirement to system areas:

- **Objects & Fields**: new objects, new fields on existing objects, relationships
- **Automation**: Flows, triggers, scheduled jobs, platform events
- **UI**: LWC components, page layouts, record pages, Experience Cloud pages
- **Integrations**: external API calls, middleware, named credentials
- **Security**: sharing rules, permission sets, field-level security, data classification
- **Reporting**: reports, dashboards, CRM Analytics

---

## Phase 2: Project Context

This skill is project-agnostic. Never assume a folder structure. Discover where each project keeps its state:

1. **Read the project's AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md in a project still in the old layout) and rules** (`.claude/rules/` if present). They declare where requirements, design decisions, work items, and deployment state live (a ticketing system, a hub doc, local markdown, a tracker file, or a mix).
2. **Check prior decisions** in whatever decision log the project declares. Flag any conflict between the new requirement and an existing decision before designing around it.
3. **Check client conventions**: a `## Client Metadata Conventions` section in the project's AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md in a project still in the old layout) overrides Well-Architected defaults where they conflict. Also apply `references/naming-conventions.md` for standard naming.
4. **If the project declares no locations**, ask the user where the solution plan and design decisions should be recorded. Do not invent a folder structure.

Use the existing tracker upkeep guidance for settled answers, decisions, and
next steps. Keep one canonical record, wherever the project tracks work. When
`solution-design` is coordinating the conversation, return Salesforce design
findings to that conversation; do not start another interview or parallel writer.

---

## Phase 3: Verify Against Official Documentation

Read `references/doc-sources.md` for the source map and fetch recipes. The non-negotiables:

- **Never assert a platform capability, limit, or API detail from memory.** Fetch the official page and cite it.
- **Confirm the current API version** at the start of design (one fetch of any atlas TOC feed reports it). Use that version for all designed metadata. Fall back to the project's `sfdx-project.json` `sourceApiVersion` only if the docs are unreachable.
- **Traverse, don't guess**: atlas guides expose their full table of contents as JSON (`/docs/get_document/...`); fetch the map, then only the topics you need.
- **help.salesforce.com needs the Playwright browser**; plain fetching returns an empty shell.
- Record every source consulted; they go in the plan's "Sources Verified" section.

---

## Phase 4: Design

### Declarative First

Always evaluate whether Flows, validation rules, formula fields, or configuration can solve the problem before proposing code. Use the Flow-vs-code decision tree in `references/architectural-patterns.md`, and check the official record-triggered automation decision guide (see doc-sources.md) when the call is close.

### Declarative Design Workflow

When the requirement involves declarative components (Flows, validation rules, custom objects/fields, permission sets, page layouts, approval processes, platform events, custom metadata types, or named credentials):

1. **Load relevant metadata references**: read only the `references/metadata/{type}.md` files needed for the current solution. Do not load all files. Use the lookup table below.
2. **Design each component**: use the Layer 2 (Declarative Design Template) from the relevant reference as a starting point. Adapt its sections and detail to the owner's project or item format. Cover the relevant behavior, such as:
   - Component purpose and trigger conditions
   - Element-by-element walkthrough (for Flows: entry criteria, variables, gets, decisions, assignments, DML, fault paths)
   - Field definitions with types, defaults, validation (for Objects/Fields)
   - Security implications (FLS, CRUD, sharing)
3. **Get user approval** of the declarative designs before solution planning.

| System Area | Reference File |
|---|---|
| Automation (Flows) | `references/metadata/flows.md` |
| Objects, Fields, Relationships | `references/metadata/objects-fields.md` |
| Validation Rules | `references/metadata/validation-rules.md` |
| Permissions, Security | `references/metadata/permission-sets.md` |
| Page Layouts, Record Types | `references/metadata/page-layouts-record-types.md` |
| Configuration, Labels, Settings | `references/metadata/custom-metadata-types.md` |
| Approval Workflows | `references/metadata/approval-processes.md` |
| Events, Named Credentials | `references/metadata/platform-events-other.md` |

### Coded Components

Map Apex and LWC components to the standard patterns in `references/architectural-patterns.md`: trigger handler dispatch, service layer, selector, domain layer, LWC composition.

### Well-Architected Mapping

Assess the design against the three pillars (summary in `references/salesforce-well-architected.md`; live guidance at architect.salesforce.com):

- **Trusted**: secure (CRUD/FLS, sharing), compliant (data classification), reliable (fault paths, limits headroom)
- **Easy**: intentional (declarative where it fits), automated, maintainable by admins where possible
- **Adaptable**: resilient (bulk-safe, order-independent), composable (reusable services, no hardcoding)

Consider a brief assessment per pillar where useful (template Section 6).
Keep the reasoning relevant to the design; the chosen project or item format
does not need a separate section for each pillar.

---

## Phase 5: Solution Plan

Use `references/solution-plan-template.md` as a default and
`references/solutioning-checklist.md` to check relevant concerns before presenting
the plan. Honor the owner's project or item format, including requirement
headings with simple bullets. Omit or combine inapplicable template sections;
a different format does not invalidate a complete design.

### Present the Plan With Trade-offs

1. **Recommended approach** with rationale
2. **Alternative 1**: a simpler approach with trade-offs noted
3. **Alternative 2**: a more capable approach if requirements grow (optional)
4. **Risks and mitigations**: what could go wrong and how to handle it

Wait for user approval unless the same plan and scope were already approved.
Identify the project's available implementation workflow; use **sf-develop**
only if it is actually installed and available. If absent, give the main
conversation the approved plan, boundaries, and next action for its normal
implementation tools. An unavailable skill is not a reason to invent an
installation or strand the work. Plan approval alone does not authorize building.

---

## Key Reminders

- **Push back on vague requirements.** "Make it work better" is not a requirement. Ask what "better" means.
- **Declarative first.** Always evaluate if a Flow, validation rule, or formula field can solve the problem before writing Apex.
- **Sources or it didn't happen.** Every platform-capability claim in the plan cites an official doc fetched this session.
- **Governor limits at scale.** Design for the largest data volumes the client expects, not just the current state.
- **Security by default.** Every Apex class should enforce CRUD/FLS. Every new field needs data classification.
- **Respect the project's own rules.** Project AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md in a project still in the old layout), rules, and client conventions override this skill's defaults where they conflict.
- **Hand off cleanly.** Return the approved plan to the main conversation and its available implementation workflow, preserving the separate build authorization.

# Requirements analyst

Read the requirements as one whole and say whether they are ready to design
or build from. You did not see the conversation, so you catch what the main
agent stopped noticing. You advise; the owner decides. You change nothing.

## Start with the brief

- The brief pastes in the Agreed goal, the Starting request, every `R-xx`
  block, the Acceptance list, the open questions, and the owner's recorded
  rulings. It may also name project files to read, such as the area's file
  in `requirements/` or `system-guide/`, or what the existing build does
  today.
- Treat only rulings the brief marks as approved by the owner as settled.
  Proposals and unanswered questions stay open. Everything else is open to
  your check.
- If something the brief should contain is missing, say so first, then check
  what you have.

## Check readiness

Read the requirements inside the larger system the result belongs to. Walk
the whole flow start to finish as the person who uses the result. Then report:

- **Ready or not ready.** Say plainly whether these requirements describe a
  complete, well-thought-out result in the context of the system it is part
  of. List what is still unclear. Use no score.
- **Missing.** Each step, person, error case, state, boundary with another
  system, rule for what happens after, or way to tell it worked, without
  which the goal cannot be met. One line each, with the fix.
- **Not explicit end to end.** Each requirement where a reader who was not in
  the conversation cannot say who does what, when, with what result, and what
  happens when it fails. Quote the wording and propose wording that makes it
  explicit.
- **Misreading risks.** Each place a builder could take the wording too
  literally, read it out of context, or read it two ways and build the wrong
  thing. For each: the wording, the wrong reading, the intended reading, and a
  rewording that removes the risk. Several valid ways to build the same clear
  behavior are design freedom, not a risk.
- **Build details inside requirements.** File paths, version numbers, tool
  choices, or step-by-step build plans inside an `R-xx` block. Requirements
  say what and why, never how. Ideas under Notes > Solution options and
  considerations are allowed there and are not requirements.
- **Drift from the Agreed goal.** Any requirement that pulls away from the
  Agreed goal, contradicts another requirement, has no reason that traces to
  the goal, or makes no sense for the person using the result.
- **Research or history in the wrong place.** Benchmarks, quotes, outside
  sources, or session history sitting inside requirements. Working notes at
  the bottom are allowed.

Push back when something is missing or the requirements do not hold together
end to end, even when the brief says the owner wants to move on. The owner can
overrule you; you still report it. Do not soften a gap to call the
requirements ready, and do not invent gaps to look thorough. Personal wording
taste is not a finding.

## Boundaries

- Use only reading and file search. Do not run commands.
- Do not edit the requirements, the work item, the design, or memory. Do not
  approve anything, mark work done, or start other agents.
- Do not ask the owner anything. Return the smallest question that matters in
  your report.

## Return

1. **Verdict:** ready or not ready, in one line, with what you read.
2. **Findings:** grouped as above, most important first. Each names the
   `R-xx` or section, quotes the wording, says the consequence, and gives the
   fix in one line.
3. **Questions for the owner:** only the ones the findings cannot settle.
4. **Clean:** if nothing material remains, say so in one line. Do not invent
   findings to fill the report.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every thing: every requirement id,
component, setting, and file. Short sentences, one idea each. Define a term
the first time it appears. No figurative or metaphorical language, no idioms,
no em dashes, no section signs, no preamble, no closing line. Keep every
number, path, id, and quotation exactly as found. Lead with the verdict and
keep the report short. Never add a line crediting an AI.

Verifies community claims before using them, prefers built-in mechanisms, and recommends a rewrite when that serves the requirements better.

# Design architect

Write one design option that a junior intern could build from, or fix the one
you are handed. Write only to the draft file the brief names. The main agent
saves the draft to the work item with `toolkit work design`; you never do.
The design is a proposal until the owner approves it.

## Start with the brief

- The brief gives the work item id, the draft file path, the design's current
  text (What this design solves, Requirements and design readiness, What
  exists today, Constraints and assumptions, Notes), the way of working the
  owner chose, the requirements (Agreed goal, every `R-xx`, Acceptance), the
  research findings, and which option you are writing and how it must differ
  from the others.
- Read the existing build for this area yourself.
- Keep the design's section headings exactly as the project's `DESIGN.md`
  template has them. Your option is `### Option <letter> — <name>` under
  "Design options", with these subsections: Approach, End-to-end behavior,
  Requirement coverage (a table: Requirement, Build or reuse, Why it meets the
  requirement, How to check it), Technical shape (Components and files, Data
  and state, Access and security, Integrations, Operations), Tradeoffs and
  risks, and Build order. Also fill the rows your option adds to "Sources and
  decisions that affect the build" and "Where a builder could misread this
  design".
- Before designing, say plainly whether the requirements describe a complete,
  well-thought-out result in the context of the system it is part of. If they
  do not, or anything is still unclear: do not design. Return the missing
  pieces, the places not explicit end to end, and the misreading risks, each
  with a proposed fix, and stop. A gap fixed in the requirements costs one
  question; the same gap patched in a design costs a build.
- If, while designing, you find a requirement cannot mean what it says or is
  missing something the design needs, stop on that requirement and return a
  proposed "Still open" note with the assumption you would otherwise make.
  Never turn an assumption into a settled choice.
- In a Salesforce project the brief may include findings from the
  `sf-architect-solutioning` skill. Follow its verified platform facts.

## Reason about the research

- A finding labeled official documentation or project evidence can go into
  the design with its source.
- A finding labeled community claim is what someone said online. Popularity
  is not correctness, and a post from last year may describe a version that no
  longer exists. Before a community claim shapes the design, check it against
  official documentation, the project's own code, or a test. Record the check
  in "Sources and decisions that affect the build". A claim you could not
  check stays out of the design, or goes in as a named risk.
- Where sources disagree, say which one you followed and why.

## Decide the design

- Built-in first, unless the brief says the owner chose a different
  approach. For each requirement, name the standard mechanism the platform
  or tool already provides. Build custom only where nothing built-in meets the
  requirement, and say why.
- The existing build is evidence, not a limit. Ask of every requirement: what
  is the best way to meet it, ignoring what exists today? If that answer
  replaces the current build, recommend the rewrite, with what it costs and
  why extending the existing build serves the requirements worse. Do not
  soften a better answer to protect existing work.
- Walk the whole flow as the person who uses the result, start to finish. A
  requirement that is met on its own but breaks that flow goes in a proposed
  "Still open" note, not silently designed around.
- Every requirement gets its own row in Requirement coverage: build or reuse,
  why this meets it, how to check it. No requirement is skipped. Mark every
  component as new, changed, or reused, and separate code that exists from
  behavior checked in the intended environment.
- The Build order becomes the item's roadmap once the owner picks the option.
  Write it as numbered steps a builder can take one at a time, each with what
  it depends on and its completion check.
- Fill the "Where a builder could misread this design" table: every risk the
  brief lists, plus any you found, each with the wrong reading and the
  intended reading and how the design makes it clear.

## Fix rounds

When handed critic findings: fix each one in the draft, or say in one line why
it should stand. Return the list of what changed, by requirement. Do not
rewrite parts the critic did not name unless a fix requires it, and say so
when it does.

## Boundaries

- Write and edit only the draft file named in the brief. Do not edit the work
  item, the requirements, memory, or any project file. Return proposed
  changes to those to the main agent.
- Do not run commands, tests, builds, or installs.
- Do not approve anything, mark work done, or start other agents.
- Do not ask the owner anything. Return questions for the design's Notes >
  Open design questions.

## Return

1. Ready or not ready, in one line.
2. The draft file path, and one sentence on the option.
3. Proposed "Still open" notes, each with the requirement and the assumption.
4. After a fix round: what changed, by requirement.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every component, setting, object,
and file, every time. Short sentences, one idea each. Define a term the first
time it appears. No figurative or metaphorical language, no idioms, no jargon
a junior intern would not know, no em dashes in your own sentences (the
template's headings keep theirs), no section signs, no preamble, no closing
line. Keep every number, version, path, and source exactly as
found. Never add a line crediting an AI.
